incidents.title: Write-heavy telemetry crushes B-tree
incidents.brief: An IoT ingest writes 90,000 small rows/s into a B-tree table. Random page updates keep the disk at 95% and p95 insert latency at 400 ms.
incidents.constraint: Writes dominate; reads are mostly recent time ranges.
incidents.question: Which storage engine fits this workload?

choices.label: Move to an LSM-tree engine with sequential flushes
choices.resultTitle: Sequential writes, calm disk
choices.resultBody: Writes land in a memtable and flush as sorted files, turning random page rewrites into sequential I/O; insert p95 falls to tens of milliseconds.

choices.label: Add secondary indexes on device_id and timestamp columns
choices.resultTitle: Each index is another write
choices.resultBody: Every insert now updates three B-trees instead of one, so write amplification and disk load rise further.

choices.label: Raise the B-tree page size from 8 KB to 64 KB
choices.resultTitle: Bigger random writes
choices.resultBody: Each random update now rewrites a larger page, so the disk moves more bytes per insert and gets busier, not calmer.

hints: Is this workload read-heavy or write-heavy?
Random in-place updates are expensive on disk.
Append first, organize later.

incidents.title: LSM reads touch every file
incidents.brief: Point lookups on the LSM store take 60 ms because each read checks dozens of SSTables for a key that usually doesn't exist.
incidents.constraint: Most lookups are for keys that are absent.
incidents.question: What cuts the wasted reads?

choices.label: Add a Bloom filter per SSTable to skip absent keys
choices.resultTitle: Most files skipped
choices.resultBody: A Bloom filter answers 'definitely not here' from memory, so a missing key costs a few filter checks instead of dozens of disk reads.

choices.label: Replace SSTables with an in-memory hash index of all keys
choices.resultTitle: Index no longer fits
choices.resultBody: Billions of keys will not fit in RAM, and a hash index loses the sorted range scans the time-series reads rely on.

choices.label: Double the memtable size so fewer lookups reach disk
choices.resultTitle: Only recent keys helped
choices.resultBody: A larger memtable holds a few more recent writes, but lookups for absent keys still scan every SSTable on disk.

hints: What does a read of a missing key cost?
You want a cheap 'definitely not here'.
A probabilistic filter per file.

variants.constraint: Workload is 97% point lookups and range scans on user_id; write throughput is under 50 ops/sec.

se-02-btree.resultTitle: B+ Tree engine delivers sub-ms point lookups and scans
se-02-btree.resultBody: With mostly read lookups and rare writes, B+ Trees avoid LSM compaction overhead and provide predictable single-seek reads.

se-02-lsm.resultTitle: LSM engine added bloom filter and multi-SSTable read amplification
se-02-lsm.resultBody: Point reads in LSM trees checked multiple SSTable levels, doubling read latencies compared to a direct B+ Tree lookup.

incidents.title: Compaction steals the disk
incidents.brief: Every afternoon LSM compaction saturates the 800 MB/s NVMe; foreground write latency spikes from 5 ms to 300 ms for 20 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Writes must stay fast even while compaction runs.
incidents.question: How should compaction be managed?

choices.label: Rate-limit compaction I/O and run heavy merges off peak
choices.resultTitle: Compaction in the background
choices.resultBody: Capping compaction bandwidth leaves headroom for foreground writes, and running the heavy merges off peak keeps p95 near 5 ms.

choices.label: Pause compaction entirely until the weekend window
choices.resultTitle: Read cost exploded
choices.resultBody: Uncompacted SSTables pile up all week, so reads check ever more files and disk usage grows with duplicate keys.

choices.label: Make writes wait for the current compaction pass
choices.resultTitle: Writes queued behind merges
choices.resultBody: Foreground writes now block on multi-minute compaction passes, turning a 300 ms spike into timeouts.

hints: Two workloads share one disk. Who wins?
Background work should stay in the background.
Budget the I/O compaction may use.

knob.label: Compaction I/O cap
knob.question: Set the compaction I/O cap so merges keep up without starving foreground writes.

low.title: Compaction falls behind
low.body: At 200 MB/s or less merges can't keep up with 55,000 writes/s; level-0 files pile past the stall threshold and the engine throttles writes, so p95 climbs toward a second.

high.title: Merges still hog the disk
high.body: Above 400 MB/s compaction takes most of the 800 MB/s the NVMe can do during the afternoon merge, so foreground writes queue behind it and p95 climbs back toward 300 ms.

good.title: Background merges, fast writes
good.body: At 250–400 MB/s compaction clears several times the incoming write volume, enough to stay ahead, while leaving about 400 MB/s for WAL writes and flushes; p95 stays near 8–12 ms.

incidents.title: Orders query scans the table
incidents.brief: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? takes 2.4 s on a 400M-row table; the DB CPU is pinned by sequential scans.
incidents.constraint: The query runs 3,000 times per second from the order-history page.
incidents.question: Now what makes the order-history query itself cheap?

choices.label: Add a B-tree index on customer_id, ordered by created_at
choices.resultTitle: Seeks instead of scans
choices.resultBody: The index finds one customer's rows in a few page reads and returns them already sorted, so the query drops from seconds to milliseconds.

choices.label: Add three read replicas and spread the scans across them
choices.resultTitle: Three slow scans instead of one
choices.resultBody: Each replica still scans 400M rows per query; you've bought three copies of the bottleneck.

choices.label: Cache every customer's full order history in Redis
choices.resultTitle: Cache misses still scan
choices.resultBody: The first read for each customer still runs the 2.4 s scan, and invalidating whole histories on every new order is costly.

hints: How many rows does the query read to find one customer?
An access path beats more copies.
Index the column in the WHERE clause.

mitigation.question: The orders DB is pinned and checkout shares it. What buys you time right now?

choices.label: Rate-limit order history to 300 req/s at the API gateway
choices.resultTitle: Scans cut by 90%, checkout breathes
choices.resultBody: The gateway lets 300 history requests/s through and returns a friendly retry to the rest, so scans fall 90% and DB CPU drops from 93% to 45%. Checkout recovers; the history page is still slow, so fix the query next.

choices.label: Restart Postgres to kill the piled-up sequential scans
choices.resultTitle: Scans return on a cold cache
choices.resultBody: Postgres was down for 40 seconds and checkout failed with it. The 3,000 req/s of scans came straight back against a cold buffer cache, and CPU is at 99% within a minute.

choices.label: Move the primary to a 2x larger instance mid-incident
choices.resultTitle: Twice the cores, same scans
choices.resultBody: The resize failed over twice for 90 seconds of errors, and a box twice the size still can't keep up: every call still scans 400M rows, so CPU settles at 88% and p95 barely moves.

incidents.title: Index slows the write path
incidents.brief: The team indexed nine columns on the events table 'just in case'. Inserts slowed from 2 ms to 25 ms and ingest is falling behind.
incidents.constraint: Only two query patterns hit this table.
incidents.question: What should they do?

choices.label: Keep indexes for the two real queries and drop the rest
choices.resultTitle: Writes fast again
choices.resultBody: Every index is updated on every insert; removing seven unused ones cuts write amplification and inserts return to a few milliseconds.

choices.label: Keep all nine and rebuild them nightly instead of on insert
choices.resultTitle: Queries read stale indexes
choices.resultBody: Most engines can't defer index maintenance; the ones that can serve queries that miss the day's rows until the rebuild.

choices.label: Move the table to faster NVMe disks and keep every index
choices.resultTitle: Inserts back under 15 ms
choices.resultBody: NVMe cut insert p95 from 25 ms to 14 ms and ingest caught up within the hour. CPU is still at 84%, because every insert still updates nine B-trees.

hints: What does each extra index cost on insert?
Indexes are for queries you actually run.
Remove what nobody reads.

incidents.title: Range scans on a hash key
incidents.brief: A time-series table is partitioned by hash(timestamp). 'Last 15 minutes' dashboards now fan out to all 64 partitions and time out.
incidents.constraint: Most reads are recent time ranges per device.
incidents.question: Which key layout fits?

choices.label: Key rows by device, then time, for one contiguous scan
choices.resultTitle: One partition, one scan
choices.resultBody: A device's recent rows sit next to each other, so the dashboard reads one small sorted range instead of querying 64 partitions.

choices.label: Increase hash(timestamp) partitions from 64 to 256
choices.resultTitle: Wider fan-out
choices.resultBody: Each range query now touches 256 partitions instead of 64, so tail latency gets worse.

choices.label: Key rows purely by timestamp to group recent data
choices.resultTitle: One hot partition
choices.resultBody: Every write for the current minute lands on the same partition, creating a write hotspot even as range reads improve.

hints: Where do one device's recent rows live today?
Hashing destroys order.
Put the range you read next to itself.

incidents.title: etcd leader elections every few minutes
incidents.brief: Kubelane's 3-node etcd runs on burstable t3.small VMs with gp2 volumes. Burst credits ran out; WAL fsync p99 is 180 ms (target under 10 ms) and leader elections fire every few minutes.
incidents.constraint: The database is only 2 GB and write volume hasn't changed; the cluster must be stable before tonight's upgrade window.
incidents.question: What brings fsync latency back under 10 ms today?

choices.label: Upsize the etcd nodes to m6i with provisioned gp3 IOPS

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: The engine was fine; the hardware under it was throttled. Fixed-performance nodes and disks remove the throttle.

choices.resultTitle: No burst credits left to run out
choices.resultBody: Members are replaced one at a time onto m6i.large nodes with gp3 volumes, whose 3,000 baseline IOPS don't depend on credits. WAL fsync p99 drops to 4 ms and elections stop. Cost: about $150 more a month; with 2 GB of data and steady writes, nothing about the engine needed to change.

choices.label: Defragment the bbolt file every hour to keep it small
choices.resultTitle: Smaller file, same throttled disk
choices.resultBody: Defragmentation reclaims some free pages but blocks writes on each member while it runs, adding its own latency spikes. Every commit still fsyncs the WAL on a volume with no burst credits, so p99 stays near 200 ms.

choices.label: Swap etcd's bbolt backend for an LSM engine with batching
choices.resultTitle: A fork for a hardware problem
choices.resultBody: etcd's storage backend isn't pluggable, so this means forking it or migrating Kubernetes to another store: weeks, not tonight. An LSM engine must also fsync its log on every commit, so a throttled gp2 volume would stall it the same way.

hints: The data is tiny and the write rate hasn't changed.
Burstable instances and gp2 volumes both slow down when credits run out.
Is the engine the problem, or what it runs on?

incidents.title: Event ingest falls 40 minutes behind
incidents.brief: The NVMe move bought three weeks. Launch-day traffic tripled events to 60,000/s; with nine indexes per insert the DB is CPU-bound at 97% and ingest lag is 40 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Budget is frozen after the NVMe upgrade; the two dashboards read by (tenant_id, ts) and by event_id.
incidents.question: What brings insert cost back down for good?

choices.label: Drop the seven indexes that no query plan has used
choices.resultTitle: Two index writes per insert, not nine
choices.resultBody: pg_stat_user_indexes shows seven indexes with zero scans. Dropping them cuts each insert from nine B-tree updates to two, CPU falls to 45%, and the backlog drains in about an hour. Cost: an ad-hoc query on those columns will now scan.

choices.label: Move the events DB to a 2x larger instance tonight
choices.resultTitle: Headroom bought with a frozen budget
choices.resultBody: Doubling cores brings CPU to 62% and the lag drains, but it adds about $1,200 a month against a frozen budget, and nine index updates per insert will eat the headroom at the next traffic jump.

choices.label: Batch inserts into 500-row multi-value statements
choices.resultTitle: Fewer statements, same index work
choices.resultBody: Round trips and commits fall 500x, so CPU drops from 97% to 89%, but each row still updates nine B-trees. The backlog now grows more slowly instead of shrinking.

hints: Disk is only 30% busy; this box is spending CPU, not IOPS.
Every index on a table is updated on every insert.
Which indexes do the two dashboards actually use?

incidents.title: Disk fills though old telemetry is deleted
incidents.brief: Since the LSM move, a nightly job deletes 7.7 billion 30-day-old rows one by one. Each delete writes a tombstone, compaction runs flat out, and disk use climbs 4% a day to 88%.
incidents.constraint: Retention is 30 days, enforced daily, and ingest can't pause.
incidents.question: How should old telemetry expire in an LSM store?

choices.label: Store each day in its own partition and drop it whole
choices.resultTitle: Expiry becomes a file delete
choices.resultBody: Rows land in a daily partition; on day 31 its files are deleted in one metadata operation, so no tombstones are written and no compaction is needed to reclaim space. Disk falls to 55% and compaction CPU with it. Cost: queries spanning days touch several partitions.

choices.label: Run a full manual compaction right after each nightly delete
choices.resultTitle: Nine hours of rewriting every night
choices.resultBody: The compaction rewrites the whole 6 TB store every night at full disk bandwidth, taking about 9 hours. Space comes back by morning, but insert p95 sits at 400 ms all night.

choices.label: Double each node's disk volume so compaction can catch up
choices.resultTitle: More room for the same tombstones
choices.resultBody: Usage drops to 44% of the bigger volume, but 7.7 billion tombstones are still written and compacted every night. CPU stays at 85% and usage keeps climbing 2% a day.

hints: In an LSM tree a delete is a write.
Space held by deleted rows only returns when compaction rewrites the files holding them.
What if expiring a day of data didn't touch individual rows at all?

incidents.title: Present-key reads slow after the Bloom rollout
incidents.brief: Bloom filters fixed absent-key lookups, but at 10 bits/key over 9 billion keys they fill 11 GB of the 16 GB block cache. Data blocks get evicted; present-key p95 went from 4 to 30 ms.
incidents.constraint: Node RAM is fixed at 32 GB, and 70% of lookups are still for absent keys.
incidents.question: How do you keep the filters without starving the data blocks?

choices.label: Partition filters so only hot filter blocks stay in cache
choices.resultTitle: Filters cached piece by piece
choices.resultBody: Each SSTable's filter is split into small blocks behind a top-level index, and only partitions for recently read key ranges stay cached, about 2 GB. Data blocks get their memory back, present-key p95 returns to 5 ms, and absent keys still skip files. Cost: a cold filter partition costs one extra read.

choices.label: Shrink the filters from 10 bits per key down to 2
choices.resultTitle: Small filters, many false positives
choices.resultBody: Filters drop to about 2 GB, but the false-positive rate jumps from ~1% to ~40%, so absent-key lookups read SSTables from disk again and p95 climbs to 45 ms.

choices.label: Skip Bloom filters on the bottom level to save memory
choices.resultTitle: Absent keys now read the last level
choices.resultBody: The bottom level holds ~90% of keys, so filter memory falls to 1.2 GB, but 70% of lookups are for absent keys and each now reads a bottom-level block from disk; p95 goes to 38 ms. That setting only pays off when most lookups find their key.

hints: Filters and data blocks compete for the same cache.
Only filters for the key ranges being read need to be in memory.
Could a filter be split and cached piece by piece, like data?

incidents.title: Size-tiered compaction consumes 50% temporary disk headroom
incidents.brief: An LSM-tree database running Size-Tiered Compaction Strategy (STCS) runs out of disk space during peak compaction of large SSTables.
incidents.constraint: Maintain stable disk footprint without requiring 50% free disk overhead.
incidents.question: Which compaction strategy reduces temporary disk amplification for large datasets?

choices.label: Migrate storage engine tables to Leveled Compaction Strategy (LCS)
choices.resultTitle: Leveled compaction capped temporary space overhead
choices.resultBody: Leveled compaction splits data into fixed-size SSTables (e.g. 160MB), requiring only ~10% temporary disk headroom instead of 50%.

choices.label: Disable background compaction entirely to preserve remaining disk space
choices.resultTitle: Read amplification exploded as SSTable count climbed
choices.resultBody: Without compaction, thousands of SSTable files accumulated, causing reads to touch hundreds of files and exhausting file handles.

choices.label: Periodically purge write-ahead logs every 60 seconds to free disk blocks
choices.resultTitle: WAL deletion caused catastrophic data loss on restart
choices.resultBody: Deleting active write-ahead logs destroyed unflushed memtable durability, resulting in missing customer transactions.

hints: STCS merges SSTables of similar size, requiring up to 100% of the table size in free temporary space.
Leveled compaction (LCS) compacts small fixed-size chunks, dramatically lowering space amplification.
Never disable compaction in LSM trees as it leads to unbounded read amplification.

incidents.title: Missing bloom filters cause excessive disk seeks on missing keys
incidents.brief: A high volume of negative lookups (querying keys that do not exist) causes 100% SSD read IOPS saturation on an LSM-tree database.
incidents.constraint: Filter out non-existent key lookups before hitting disk without inflating RAM usage.
incidents.question: What storage engine index data structure prevents reading SSTables for missing keys?

choices.label: Configure 10 bits per key Bloom filters on all SSTables in memory
choices.resultTitle: Bloom filters deflected 99% of negative disk lookups
choices.resultBody: Bloom filters quickly prove key absence in memory, eliminating unnecessary disk block reads for missing records.

choices.label: Execute linear full scans on all SSTables to guarantee key verification
choices.resultTitle: Full scans collapsed storage IO bandwidth completely
choices.resultBody: Reading every SSTable block sequentially maximized disk read saturation and throttled all other concurrent queries.

choices.label: Bypass operating system page cache to read directly from raw block devices
choices.resultTitle: Direct I/O eliminated caching benefits for hot index blocks
choices.resultBody: Disabling OS buffer caches forced every metadata lookup to hit the physical SSD, doubling overall latency.

hints: LSM trees must check multiple SSTable files unless an in-memory filter verifies the key is absent.
Bloom filters provide a fast probabilistic check with zero false negatives.
Allocating ~10 bits per key in RAM provides approximately a 1% false positive rate.

incidents.title: Write stalls trigger when memtable flush falls behind WAL
incidents.brief: A massive bulk ingest causes active memtables to fill faster than background flush threads can write SSTables to disk, triggering a full engine write stall.
incidents.constraint: Absorb write ingest bursts without stalling incoming client API calls.
incidents.question: How should memtable and flush concurrency be tuned to eliminate write stalls?

choices.label: Increase max_write_buffer_number and allocate dedicated flush worker threads
choices.resultTitle: Expanded buffer pipeline absorbed ingest surges
choices.resultBody: Allowing more immutable memtables in queue and parallelizing flush threads prevented the engine from freezing incoming writes.

choices.label: Reduce write buffer size to 4MB so flushes trigger more frequently
choices.resultTitle: Tiny memtables generated millions of tiny SSTable files
choices.resultBody: Flushing tiny files overwhelmed the L0 compaction queue, triggering immediate write stalls and severe compaction debt.

choices.label: Drop writes automatically whenever memtable memory utilization crosses 80%
choices.resultTitle: Dropping writes caused unrecoverable data ingestion loss
choices.resultBody: Silently dropping customer data violated durability guarantees instead of safely backpressuring producers.

hints: LSM engines stall writes when the number of unflushed immutable memtables exceeds limits.
Increasing write buffer count provides headroom to absorb high-throughput write bursts.
Parallel background flush threads ensure data writes to disk as fast as memory accumulates.

incidents.title: B-Tree page split churn fragments random write workload
incidents.brief: A relational database using B+ Tree storage suffers 8x write amplification and 35% empty page bloat under heavy random UUID inserts.
incidents.constraint: Reduce page splits and fragmentation without changing the core relational database schema.
incidents.question: How should index fill factors or insert ordering be configured to reduce page splits?

choices.label: Lower index fill factor to 70% to reserve space for random leaf inserts
choices.resultTitle: Adjusted fill factor stopped recursive page splitting
choices.resultBody: Leaving 30% free headroom on leaf pages allows random inserts to land without triggering expensive page allocations.

choices.label: Set fill factor to 100% to pack index pages completely full on disk
choices.resultTitle: 100% fill factor triggered continuous page splits
choices.resultBody: Every single random insert into a completely full leaf forced a 50/50 page split, doubling disk I/O and lock contention.

choices.label: Drop primary key indexes and perform table lookups with table scans
choices.resultTitle: Dropping primary indexes made queries unacceptably slow
choices.resultBody: Removing indexes forced every single point query to scan millions of rows, crippling system responsiveness.

hints: Random primary keys (like UUIDv4) insert into arbitrary leaf pages of a B+ Tree.
When a target page is 100% full, the database must split the page and rewrite parent pointers.
Lowering fill factor leaves spare slots for random inserts, dramatically reducing splits.

incidents.title: Unthrottled compaction saturates NVMe IOPS during business peak
incidents.brief: Midday compaction kicks in with unconstrained disk read/write bandwidth, pushing disk utilization to 100% and degrading p99 user request latencies.
incidents.constraint: Keep user read latency under 50ms while ensuring compaction still completes.
incidents.question: How should compaction background I/O bandwidth be throttled?

choices.label: Enforce compaction rate-limiting token bucket at 100MB/s on disk I/O
choices.resultTitle: Compaction rate limiting preserved interactive IOPS
choices.resultBody: Throttling background compaction I/O ensures user-facing read operations get priority access to disk controllers.

choices.label: Raise compaction thread process priority to realtime above query threads
choices.resultTitle: Realtime compaction starved all interactive customer queries
choices.resultBody: Elevating compaction priority caused background processes to preempt client threads, crashing user request fulfillment.

choices.label: Reboot storage nodes whenever disk IOPS utilization exceeds 90%
choices.resultTitle: Reboots restarted interrupted compactions from zero
choices.resultBody: Rebooting the node aborted active compactions, only for the same heavy compactions to re-trigger immediately on startup.

hints: Compaction is an asynchronous background maintenance job that should yield to foreground traffic.
Rate limiting compaction bandwidth prevents disk saturation without stopping data cleanup.
RocksDB and Cassandra both provide rate-limiting controls for compaction I/O throughput.
